nameStory: The roughleaf dogwood gets its name from its distinctively textured leaves that feel noticeably rough and sandpapery to the touch, setting it apart from its smoother-leaved dogwood cousins. The 'dogwood' part of the name comes from 'dag wood' - 'dag' being an old English word for skewer, referring to how the hard wood was once used to make pointed tools and daggers.
description: Roughleaf dogwood is a small deciduous tree or large shrub that reaches 15-25 feet tall with a spread of 10-15 feet. It's primarily a Midwestern native that's quite uncommon in New England, with only a handful of sightings recorded in our region. This dogwood produces clusters of small, near-white four-petaled flowers in summer, followed by white berries that ripen in late summer and fall. It tends to form dense thickets that provide excellent wildlife cover.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: The leaves feel distinctly rough and sandpapery when you run your fingers across the surface - this sandpaper texture is the plant's signature feature that gives it its common name.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small near-white flowers with four distinct petals appear in flat-topped clusters during summer months, lacking the large showy bracts of flowering dogwood.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small white berries ripen from August through October, often persisting on branches and providing a key identification feature in late season.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, spreading thickets rather than growing as a single-trunked tree, creating impenetrable wildlife cover that can spread 10-15 feet wide.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Mature bark develops shallow furrows and a grayish-brown color, though the rough leaf texture remains the most reliable identifying feature.

habitat: In New England, roughleaf dogwood is extremely rare and most likely found as an escaped ornamental or naturalized planting rather than a true wild native. When present, look for it along forest edges, in disturbed areas, or near developed areas where it may have been planted as a landscape buffer. It prefers well-drained soils and can tolerate various light conditions from partial shade to full sun.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge with their characteristic rough texture already apparent, making this the best time to feel the diagnostic sandpaper-like leaf surface.
seasonality.summer: Small clusters of near-white four-petaled flowers bloom during the warmest months, providing the most obvious visual identification feature during this season.
seasonality.fall: White berries ripen and may persist on branches, while leaves may develop modest fall color before dropping, leaving the branching pattern visible.
seasonality.winter: Bare branches show the dense, thicket-forming growth habit, and any persistent white berries provide identification clues along with the overall branching structure.

funFact: Over forty different bird species feast on roughleaf dogwood berries, making a single thicket a veritable bird buffet that can attract everything from cardinals to cedar waxwings throughout the fall migration season.
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with gray dogwood, but the roughleaf dogwood's sandpaper-textured leaves are unmistakable once you touch them - gray dogwood leaves feel smooth and typical. Memory trick: 'Rough by name, rough by touch.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'roughleaf dogwood,' this species is extremely uncommon in New England and is primarily a Great Plains and Midwestern native. Most dogwoods you encounter in New England will be other species, so finding a true roughleaf dogwood would be quite a botanical discovery worth documenting.
compareHints: Among New England dogwoods, roughleaf dogwood is unique for its sandpaper-textured leaves - no other dogwood species in our region has this distinctive rough feel. Gray dogwood is most similar in size and white berry color, but has smooth leaves and slightly different flower timing. The small summer flowers also distinguish it from flowering dogwood's large spring blooms with showy white bracts.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its tree and shrub dogwood relatives, Canadian bunchberry is the only dogwood in New England that grows as a tiny herbaceous perennial on the forest floor.
Among dogwoods, this is the only one in New England with alternate leaves - all others have opposite leaves.
Among New England's dogwoods, red osier is the wetland specialist with the most colorful bark.
Among New England's dogwoods, silky dogwood is unique for its distinctly fuzzy leaf undersides - run your finger underneath any dogwood leaf, and only silky dogwood will feel soft and velvety.
Among New England's dogwoods, flowering dogwood is unique for its large, showy white bracts and tree-like size.

Among New England's dogwoods, gray dogwood is unique for its white berries on red stems - flowering dogwood has red berries, red osier dogwood has white berries on white stems, and silky dogwood has blue berries.
Among New England dogwoods, round-leaved dogwood is unique for its combination of rounded leaf tips and rough leaf texture.
Among dogwoods, kousa is unique for its late bloom time, pointed bracts, and strawberry-like fruits.

Among New England dogwoods, blue-fruited dogwood is distinguished by its true blue berries - red osier dogwood has white berries, gray dogwood has white berries on red stems, and silky dogwood has blue-white berries.
Unlike our native flowering dogwood with its large white bracts, cornelian cherry has tiny yellow flowers in clusters.
Common dogwood stands out from other New England dogwoods primarily by its intensely colored winter stems - most of our native dogwoods have gray, brown, or only mildly reddish winter bark.

Among dogwoods, Tatarian dogwood's red stems are most similar to native red osier dogwood, but Tatarian tends to have more orange-red coloring and is found in drier garden settings rather than wetlands.

Korean cornel dogwood differs from most other dogwoods in New England by blooming very early with small yellow flowers rather than white ones, and by producing oval red fruits rather than round blue or white berries.
